answer: I'd like to talk about a morning I would honestly rather forget. A time I was embarrassingly late was for an important job interview a few years ago, just after I had finished university. The interview was in Dhaka, so I stayed the night before at my elder sister's flat, thinking that would give me plenty of time. I had planned everything carefully, but on the day, the traffic was absolutely [[horrendous]] due to an unexpected road closure. I sat helplessly in a CNG auto-rickshaw, watching the minutes tick away, growing more [[jittery]] by the second. I kept checking my watch every thirty seconds, as if that would somehow make the traffic move. I called ahead to apologise, which was [[mortifying]], and eventually arrived nearly half an hour late, [[flustered]] and sweating. To my relief, the interviewers were surprisingly understanding, and the interview went reasonably well despite my terrible start. One of them even joked that being stuck in Dhaka traffic was practically a local tradition, which helped me relax a little. As for how I felt, I was ashamed at first and then hugely relieved. However, the whole experience taught me a valuable lesson about leaving a proper buffer for the unexpected. Since then I have become almost [[obsessive]] about arriving early for anything important. Honestly, the stress of that day was enough to change my habits for good. I now always plan for delays, because I never want to feel that particular kind of panic again. It was a bad day, but I am oddly grateful for it now.

followUps.q: Did you get the job in the end?
followUps.answer: No, I didn't, though I don't think it was only because I was late. Luckily, a few weeks later I was offered my current job at the consultancy, which suits me much better anyway.

followUps.q: Are people in your country usually on time?
followUps.answer: Honestly, not always. Traffic in the cities is so unpredictable that people tend to be quite relaxed about being a little late. For formal things like interviews, though, punctuality really matters.

note: Set in Dhaka (stayed at elder sister's flat, CNG instead of taxi); 'anxious' and 'understanding' were plain, replaced by 'jittery', 'mortifying', 'flustered'.
